title: Research Progress and Translational Applications of Experimental Models in Colorectal Cancer: A Survey Outline

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Classification of Experimental Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Biological Basis of Colorectal Cancer Modeling
subsections.content:
The biological basis of colorectal cancer (CRC) modeling lies in the multistep evolution of normal intestinal epithelium into adenoma and invasive carcinoma through the cumulative disruption of core growth-control pathways. Foundational genetic analyses established recurrent alterations in APC/WNT signaling, KRAS-driven mitogenic signaling, TP53-mediated genome surveillance, and TGF-β pathway components as major determinants of colorectal tumorigenesis, providing a mechanistic scaffold for experimental models that recapitulate initiation and progression ref [1], ref [2]. These lesions arise within a highly ordered epithelial system sustained by crypt-resident stem cells, making tissue architecture, lineage hierarchy, and proliferative compartmentalization central biological features that models must capture ref [3].

CRC is also biologically heterogeneous. Large-scale molecular profiling has shown that tumors differ in mutation burden, chromosomal instability, microsatellite instability, CpG island methylation, and transcriptomic state, with important consequences for prognosis, immune contexture, and therapeutic response ref [4], ref [5]. Accordingly, biologically informative models should reflect not only driver genotypes but also the broader molecular subtypes and evolutionary trajectories seen in patients. This is especially relevant for modeling serrated versus conventional pathways, metastatic competence, and treatment resistance.

A further rationale for CRC modeling is the dependence of malignant behavior on the surrounding ecosystem. Intestinal inflammation can promote tumor initiation and progression, while stromal, vascular, and immune components shape invasion, clonal selection, and drug sensitivity ref [6]. More recent organoid-based approaches underscore that epithelial-intrinsic programs can be reconstructed ex vivo, but also highlight the need to reintroduce microenvironmental interactions when studying advanced disease biology ref [7]. Thus, the biological validity of any CRC model depends on how faithfully it represents epithelial genetics, cellular hierarchy, and tumor–microenvironment crosstalk.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Classification of Experimental Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Historical Development of Colorectal Cancer Models
subsections.content:
The historical trajectory of colorectal cancer (CRC) modeling mirrors broader shifts in cancer biology, from descriptive pathology to mechanistic and translational experimentation. Early work relied heavily on chemically induced rodent tumors, especially with dimethylhydrazine and azoxymethane, which provided reproducible in vivo systems for studying adenoma formation, progression, and the influence of diet and inflammation on colonic carcinogenesis ref [8]. In parallel, the development of transplantable and then continuously propagated human CRC cell lines created tractable in vitro platforms for molecular and pharmacologic studies, exemplified by the establishment of widely used lines such as HT-29 ref [9].

A major conceptual turning point came with the genetic dissection of human CRC. The adenoma-carcinoma sequence and its associated accumulation of mutations provided a framework for engineering models around defined driver events ref [10]. This logic was rapidly translated into genetically engineered mice, most notably the ApcMin model, which demonstrated that mutation of a gatekeeper tumor suppressor could be sufficient to initiate intestinal neoplasia and thereby linked murine genetics to human disease mechanisms ref [11]. These models shifted the field from carcinogen-based phenomenology toward pathway-centered experimentation.

More recent decades have emphasized fidelity to human tumor heterogeneity and clinical behavior. Patient-derived xenografts enabled propagation of primary CRC tissue in immunodeficient mice while preserving many histologic and genomic features of the source tumors ref [12]. Subsequently, long-term organoid culture from normal and neoplastic human intestinal epithelium allowed genetically controlled, patient-specific ex vivo modeling, creating a bridge between reductionist cell systems and in vivo studies ref [13]. Together, these successive platforms illustrate how CRC models have evolved toward increasing molecular precision, cellular complexity, and translational relevance.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Classification of Experimental Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.content:
Experimental models of colorectal cancer (CRC) can be organized into four broad categories that capture complementary levels of biological complexity. First, conventional in vitro systems, especially immortalized human CRC cell lines, provide tractable platforms for interrogating oncogenic signaling, drug response, and genotype–phenotype relationships, although prolonged adaptation to plastic and serum can reduce tissue architecture and clonal heterogeneity relative to patient tumors ref [14].

Second, ex vivo three-dimensional models, particularly organoids derived from normal colon or CRC tissue, preserve epithelial polarity, stem-cell hierarchies, and many patient-specific genomic features, thereby bridging reductionist cell culture and in vivo disease biology ref [15], ref [16]. Third, in vivo animal models include carcinogen-induced and genetically engineered mouse models that reproduce defined steps of adenoma formation, invasive progression, and interactions with the immune and stromal microenvironment; landmark Apc-based models have been especially important for studying WNT-driven intestinal tumorigenesis ref [11], ref [17].

Fourth, transplantation-based systems encompass cell line xenografts, patient-derived xenografts, and orthotopic implantation approaches. These models are widely used for therapeutic testing because they retain greater architectural and molecular fidelity than standard cell lines, although host immunodeficiency limits analysis of intact anti-tumor immunity ref [18]. Together, these categories form a practical taxonomy: in vitro models maximize experimental control, organoids improve human tissue relevance, engineered and carcinogen-driven animals model tumor evolution in situ, and xenograft platforms strengthen translational drug evaluation ref [13].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Classification of Experimental Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.content:
Evaluation of colorectal cancer (CRC) models should begin with fidelity to the human disease across genetic, histopathologic, and evolutionary dimensions. High-value models reproduce recurrent driver alterations such as APC, KRAS, TP53, and mismatch-repair defects, while also recapitulating glandular architecture, invasive behavior, and intratumoral heterogeneity ref [2], ref [19]. Because CRC develops through multiple routes—including chromosomal instability, microsatellite instability, and inflammation-associated tumorigenesis—model validity depends not on generic resemblance to cancer, but on alignment with a defined molecular subtype or disease trajectory ref [20].

A second criterion is preservation of the tumor microenvironment and host context. Many reductionist systems offer experimental control but incompletely capture stromal signaling, immune interactions, microbial influences, and metastatic niche formation, all of which shape therapy response and progression in CRC ref [21], ref [22]. Conversely, genetically engineered and orthotopic in vivo models often provide stronger contextual validity, though at the cost of lower throughput and greater complexity. Practical considerations therefore matter: reproducibility, scalability, time to readout, amenability to genome editing or drug testing, and the extent to which a model predicts patient response should all be weighed explicitly ref [19], ref [23].

Finally, evaluative criteria should include translational robustness. Patient-derived organoids and xenografts are particularly useful when preservation of interpatient diversity and pharmacologic response is prioritized, but they may drift under selection or lose immune competence depending on culture or host conditions ref [23], ref [24]. In practice, model assessment is strongest when these criteria are treated as complementary rather than hierarchical, motivating deliberate use of model ensembles rather than reliance on any single platform.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Classification of Experimental Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Matching Model Type to Research Question
subsections.content:
Selecting an experimental model for colorectal cancer (CRC) should begin with the biological question rather than with technical convenience. Genetically engineered mouse models are most informative when the objective is to study stepwise tumor initiation, tissue context, and host-level effects of canonical driver pathways such as APC/WNT, KRAS, TP53, and TGF-β signaling, because these systems preserve intestinal architecture, immune competence, and organismal physiology ref [25], ref [26]. By contrast, xenografts and patient-derived xenografts are better suited to evaluating tumor maintenance, intertumoral heterogeneity, and in vivo drug response, although murine stromal replacement and immunodeficiency limit their value for studying native immune interactions ref [27].

For mechanistic studies requiring experimental tractability and rapid perturbation, 2D cell lines remain useful, especially for pathway dissection, genetic screening, and pharmacologic benchmarking. However, their long-term adaptation to plastic and restricted microenvironmental complexity can distort differentiation state and therapeutic vulnerability. Three-dimensional organoid cultures provide a stronger match when the research question concerns patient-specific genotype-phenotype relationships, epithelial hierarchy, clonal evolution, or ex vivo precision testing, while still enabling genome engineering and medium-throughput assays ref [13], ref [16].

Questions centered on metastasis, stromal crosstalk, and treatment response across scales often require combined model pipelines rather than a single platform. For example, organoids can nominate genotype-dependent mechanisms, orthotopic or metastatic transplantation models can test dissemination and colonization, and matched patient-derived models can support translational validation. More recently, organoid co-culture and microphysiological systems have been developed to capture immune and mesenchymal components that are underrepresented in epithelial-only models ref [28]. Thus, model choice is best understood as a problem of fit between experimental resolution, biological complexity, and intended translational endpoint.

subsections.section_title: In Vitro and Ex Vivo Experimental Platforms for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.content:
Conventional two-dimensional (2D) colorectal cancer (CRC) cell lines remain the most accessible in vitro platform for mechanistic and screening studies because they are inexpensive, scalable, genetically tractable, and compatible with standardized assays. Historic panels such as those established from human colon carcinomas provided durable models for interrogating growth control, differentiation, and drug response under tightly controlled conditions ref [29], ref [30]. Their translational value was further enhanced by large-scale molecular annotation showing that commonly used lines capture many recurrent genomic alterations in CRC, including APC, KRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA, SMAD4, and TP53 lesions, thereby enabling genotype-directed experimentation ref [31].

A major strength of 2D systems is experimental reproducibility: clonal expansion, straightforward transfection or genome editing, and suitability for high-throughput pharmacologic testing make them ideal for dissecting signaling dependencies such as WNT/EGFR/MAPK and PI3K pathway interactions. Integrative analyses across large cell-line collections have shown that genomic features can predict sensitivity to targeted agents, supporting the use of CRC cell lines for biomarker discovery and hypothesis generation before validation in more complex models ref [32], ref [33]. These models have also been central to molecular subtype studies, although subtype representation is uneven and often biased toward highly proliferative epithelial states ref [34].

Their limitations are equally well recognized. Long-term passage can select for culture-adapted clones, 2D monolayers lack native extracellular matrix architecture and stromal, immune, and microbial interactions, and some legacy lines suffer from misidentification or cross-contamination, necessitating routine authentication and mycoplasma testing ref [35]. Accordingly, 2D CRC cell lines are best viewed as foundational reductionist systems whose strengths in throughput and manipulability complement, rather than replace, organoid, co-culture, and ex vivo tissue platforms.

subsections.section_title: In Vitro and Ex Vivo Experimental Platforms for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.content:
Three-dimensional colorectal cancer models bridge the gap between reductionist monolayer cultures and more complex tissue-based systems. Multicellular spheroids generated from established cell lines better reproduce diffusion gradients of oxygen, nutrients, metabolites, and drugs, thereby capturing proliferation heterogeneity, hypoxic cores, and treatment resistance that are poorly modeled in two dimensions. As a result, spheroids have been widely adopted for mechanistic studies of invasion, radiochemotherapy response, and intermediate-throughput therapeutic screening in colorectal cancer ref [36], ref [37].

Organoid systems extend this concept by enabling long-term growth of self-organizing epithelial structures from normal intestinal crypts and colorectal tumors in defined extracellular matrix and niche-factor conditions. Foundational studies showed that Lgr5-positive intestinal stem cells can generate crypt-villus organoids ex vivo and that human colorectal cancer organoids preserve key histologic and genetic features of the source lesions ref [15], ref [38]. Subsequent work established living biobanks of patient-derived colorectal cancer organoids, demonstrating retention of interpatient molecular diversity and variable drug sensitivities with potential translational relevance ref [16], ref [23].

Despite these advantages, organoid cultures remain predominantly epithelial and incompletely represent stromal, immune, vascular, and microbial influences. Matrix dependence, selective growth conditions, and clonal drift can also bias representation of the parental tumor. Accordingly, spheroid and organoid systems are best viewed as experimentally tractable platforms that complement, rather than replace, co-culture, microfluidic, and ex vivo tissue models when studying microenvironment-dependent colorectal cancer biology ref [23], ref [39].

subsections.section_title: In Vitro and Ex Vivo Experimental Platforms for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.content:
Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) have emerged as a central ex vivo platform for colorectal cancer because they preserve key histologic, genomic, and functional features of the donor tumor while allowing scalable expansion under defined culture conditions. Early studies showed that colorectal tumor organoids can be established efficiently from surgical and biopsy material and maintain patient-specific mutational landscapes, including APC, KRAS, TP53, and SMAD4 alterations, across passages, supporting their use for mechanistic studies and medium-throughput drug testing ref [16], ref [38]. Comparative analyses further indicate that PDO collections recapitulate much of the interpatient transcriptional and pharmacologic heterogeneity seen in clinical disease, making them attractive complements to conventional cell lines ref [23].

Biobanking has extended the value of PDOs from single-patient models to population-scale resources. Living organoid biobanks generated from colorectal cancer specimens, including primary and metastatic lesions, have enabled standardized cryopreservation, re-expansion, and retrospective linkage to clinical and molecular annotation ref [38], ref [40]. Such repositories support comparative studies of treatment sensitivity, clonal diversity, and genotype-drug associations, and they are increasingly used to benchmark precision oncology workflows. Importantly, matched normal and tumor organoids can often be banked from the same patient, facilitating studies of therapeutic index and epithelial transformation ref [16], ref [41].

Despite these strengths, PDO biobanks also have limitations. Standard epithelial organoid culture enriches for tumor-cell intrinsic phenotypes but incompletely captures stromal, immune, and vascular influences, and long-term passage may shift subclonal representation or select for culture-adapted states. Accordingly, recent work has emphasized harmonized derivation protocols, quality-control genomics, and integration with co-culture or xenograft validation to improve translational fidelity ref [40], ref [42]. In colorectal cancer, PDO biobanks are therefore best viewed as a renewable, patient-linked backbone for preclinical discovery rather than a complete surrogate for the native tumor ecosystem.

subsections.section_title: In Vitro and Ex Vivo Experimental Platforms for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.content:
Co-culture and microenvironment-integrated models address a central limitation of epithelial-only colorectal cancer systems by incorporating stromal, immune, or vascular compartments that shape growth, invasion, and treatment response. Fibroblast-containing systems are particularly informative because cancer-associated fibroblasts remodel extracellular matrix, secrete paracrine factors, and can induce drug resistance or invasive phenotypes not observed in monoculture. Early three-dimensional organotypic models showed that stromal myofibroblasts enhance colorectal cancer cell invasion through hepatocyte growth factor and matrix-dependent signaling, illustrating how tumor behavior emerges from reciprocal epithelial-stromal interactions rather than intrinsic tumor cell programs alone [1,2].

Organoid-based co-cultures have extended these concepts into more patient-relevant settings. Human intestinal and colorectal cancer organoids can be maintained with niche-supporting mesenchymal populations, enabling interrogation of Wnt, BMP, and growth factor crosstalk that is otherwise supplied exogenously in reductionist culture conditions [3]. At the same time, direct co-culture of patient-derived tumor organoids with autologous lymphocytes has created tractable platforms for studying antigen-specific T-cell recognition and immunotherapy response ex vivo, offering a bridge between organoid biobanking and functional precision oncology [4].

Microenvironment integration also includes vasculature and multicellular matrices. Perfusable vascularized micro-tumor systems and engineered three-dimensional matrices have been used to model endothelial interactions, intravasation-associated phenotypes, and spatial gradients in oxygen or nutrients that influence colorectal cancer invasion and drug sensitivity [5,6]. Although these platforms remain more technically demanding and less standardized than conventional organoid assays, they are increasingly valuable for dissecting context-dependent mechanisms and for testing combination strategies that target both malignant cells and their supporting niche.

subsections.section_title: In Vitro and Ex Vivo Experimental Platforms for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.content:
Organ-on-a-chip and related microfluidic systems extend conventional colorectal cancer culture by imposing controlled fluid flow, chemical gradients, and multicellular compartmentalization that are difficult to reproduce in static plates. These platforms are particularly valuable for modeling epithelial polarization, barrier function, and drug transport, while enabling continuous imaging and sampling of secreted factors. A foundational advance was the gut-on-a-chip concept, which showed that microengineered flow and mechanical cues can drive intestinal epithelial morphogenesis and differentiated function beyond standard Transwell culture ref [48].

For colorectal cancer, microfluidic devices have been adapted to interrogate invasion, intravasation, and organ-specific metastasis under physiologically relevant shear stress. In particular, tumor-endothelium interfaces and vascularized chips permit analysis of cancer cell extravasation and stromal interactions in ways that bridge reductionist in vitro assays and animal models ref [49], ref [50]. More recent microphysiological systems have incorporated patient-derived colorectal organoids, allowing parallel assessment of growth dynamics and drug response in perfused settings that better capture nutrient delivery and microenvironmental heterogeneity ref [51].

Despite these strengths, adoption remains constrained by fabrication complexity, limited standardization, and challenges in integrating immune, microbial, and matrix components over extended culture periods. Nevertheless, advances in modular body-on-a-chip designs and increasingly robust intestine-on-chip workflows suggest a growing role for these systems in preclinical pharmacology, especially for studying metastatic colonization, treatment penetration, and patient-specific therapeutic vulnerabilities ref [52], ref [53].

subsections.section_title: In Vitro and Ex Vivo Experimental Platforms for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.subsection_title: Ex Vivo Tissue Slice and Explant Models
subsections.content:
Ex vivo tissue slice and explant models preserve native colorectal cancer architecture, including epithelial, stromal, vascular, and resident immune compartments, and therefore occupy an important intermediate position between reductionist culture systems and in vivo studies. Precision-cut or manually prepared tumor slices retain spatial heterogeneity and cell-cell interactions over short culture windows, enabling interrogation of drug response, signaling dynamics, and biomarker modulation in clinically relevant tissue contexts. Early work established the feasibility of maintaining human colorectal tumor explants for pharmacodynamic studies and demonstrated that ex vivo responses could be quantified with histologic and molecular readouts ref [54], ref [55].

A major strength of these platforms is their capacity to test therapeutic perturbations while conserving microenvironmental determinants that are difficult to reconstruct in organoids or 2D culture. Colorectal cancer slice cultures have been used to examine proliferation, apoptosis, and pathway inhibition after standard cytotoxics or targeted agents, while also allowing parallel assessment of matched normal tissue and intratumoral variability ref [55], ref [56]. Related ex vivo approaches in patient-derived cancer tissue slices have further highlighted their utility for short-term functional precision oncology, especially when integrated with multiplex imaging and genomic profiling ref [57], ref [58].

However, these models remain constrained by limited viability, absence of systemic inputs, and sensitivity to ischemic injury, slice thickness, and culture conditions. Standardization of procurement, media composition, oxygenation, and analytic endpoints is therefore critical for reproducibility. Even with these limitations, colorectal explant systems provide a high-content platform for validating candidate therapies, studying stromal and immune influences on treatment response, and bridging mechanistic discovery to translational testing ref [56], ref [58], ref [59].

subsections.section_title: In Vivo Models of Colorectal Cancer: From Tumor Initiation to Metastatic Dissemination
subsections.content:
Chemically induced models were among the earliest in vivo systems used to study colorectal tumorigenesis and remain valuable because they reproduce multistep epithelial transformation in an immunocompetent host. The colon-specific carcinogen azoxymethane (AOM), and its precursor 1,2-dimethylhydrazine, generate O6-methylguanine DNA adducts and induce adenomas and adenocarcinomas with histologic features resembling human sporadic disease, including frequent activation of Wnt signaling and mutations in Ctnnb1 or Kras rather than Apc loss ref [60], ref [61]. These models are relatively inexpensive and experimentally tractable, making them useful for studies of initiation, promotion, and chemoprevention.

A major advance was the combination of AOM with dextran sodium sulfate (DSS), which couples mutagenic injury to chronic colitis and thereby models inflammation-associated colorectal cancer. This protocol accelerates tumor development, increases multiplicity, and permits mechanistic interrogation of epithelial–immune crosstalk, cytokine signaling, barrier dysfunction, and microbiota-dependent effects ref [62], ref [63]. Because tumor formation depends strongly on DSS dose, strain background, and microbial composition, the model is highly sensitive to environmental modifiers but can also suffer from inter-laboratory variability.

The main strengths of chemically induced systems are their intact stroma and immunity, broad applicability across strains, and suitability for prevention and inflammation studies. Their limitations include variable penetrance, heterogeneous mutation spectra, and generally limited spontaneous metastatic dissemination compared with orthotopic or genetically engineered approaches ref [64], ref [65]. Accordingly, these models are best viewed as complementary to GEMMs and transplantation systems when studying the transition from early mucosal injury to invasive colorectal cancer.

subsections.section_title: In Vivo Models of Colorectal Cancer: From Tumor Initiation to Metastatic Dissemination
subsections.content:
Genetically engineered mouse models (GEMMs) have been central to defining colorectal cancer (CRC) as a stepwise, genotype-driven disease in vivo. The foundational Apc mutant models established that deregulated Wnt signaling is sufficient to initiate intestinal adenoma formation, closely mirroring the earliest genetic lesion in human CRC; notably, ApcMin/+ mice develop multiple intestinal neoplasms, while targeted Apc loss in the colon better models large-bowel tumorigenesis ref [11], ref [66]. These systems enabled precise interrogation of tumor initiation within an intact epithelium, stromal compartment, and immune microenvironment.

Subsequent compound GEMMs incorporated alterations in Kras, Trp53, Tgfbr2, and DNA mismatch repair to model progression from benign adenoma toward invasive and, in some settings, metastatic carcinoma. Conditional activation of oncogenic Kras together with Apc loss accelerates adenoma growth and dysplasia, whereas additional disruption of TGF-β and p53 pathways promotes invasion and dissemination, thereby recapitulating key features of advanced CRC ref [67], ref [68]. Parallel mismatch-repair-deficient models, including Msh2- or Mlh1-deficient mice, have been especially informative for studying hypermutated, microsatellite-unstable disease and its interaction with host immunity ref [69], ref [70].

Despite their mechanistic value, GEMMs also have limitations: many develop predominantly small-intestinal rather than colonic lesions, show variable latency, and incompletely capture the genomic complexity and organotropism of human metastatic CRC. Newer inducible and tissue-restricted alleles, including colon-specific Cre strategies, partly address these issues and improve the modeling of temporal evolution and site-specific disease ref [66], ref [71]. Overall, GEMMs remain indispensable for linking defined driver combinations to adenoma-carcinoma progression, immune surveillance, and therapeutic response in a whole-organism context.

subsections.section_title: In Vivo Models of Colorectal Cancer: From Tumor Initiation to Metastatic Dissemination
subsections.content:
Syngeneic and allograft models occupy an important middle ground between genetically engineered systems and xenografts, because murine colorectal cancer cells are implanted into immunocompetent hosts of the same genetic background. This preserves tumor–immune crosstalk, stromal recruitment, and therapy-induced inflammatory responses while offering substantially greater speed and experimental flexibility than de novo autochthonous models. Widely used transplantable lines include CT26, derived from BALB/c colon carcinoma, and MC38, a chemically induced C57BL/6 colon adenocarcinoma line that has become a benchmark for immuno-oncology studies because of its relatively high mutational burden and responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade ref [64], ref [72], ref [73].

These models can be deployed subcutaneously for rapid tumor growth assays or orthotopically to better capture local invasion and spontaneous dissemination. Surgical cecal or rectal implantation of syngeneic tumor fragments or cells improves anatomical fidelity and can reproduce liver and lung metastasis more effectively than ectopic grafting, thereby enabling studies of colonization routes and organ-specific immune regulation ref [74], ref [75]. In parallel, comparative molecular analyses have shown that commonly used murine colorectal allografts differ markedly in antigenicity, WNT/MAPK pathway activity, and myeloid or lymphoid infiltration, underscoring that model choice strongly shapes conclusions about drug response and immune escape ref [73], ref [76].

The principal strengths of syngeneic/allograft systems are throughput, reproducibility, and compatibility with immunotherapy, radiation, and combination treatment experiments. Their main limitations are equally important: long-term in vitro passaging, non-physiologic implantation when used ectopically, and species-specific divergence from human colorectal cancer all constrain translational interpretation. Accordingly, they are most informative when integrated with orthotopic approaches and complemented by genetically engineered or patient-derived models ref [75], ref [76], ref [77].

subsections.section_title: In Vivo Models of Colorectal Cancer: From Tumor Initiation to Metastatic Dissemination
subsections.content:
Xenograft models, generated by implanting established human colorectal cancer (CRC) cell lines into immunodeficient mice, have provided a scalable platform for testing tumor growth kinetics, drug response, and biomarker-driven interventions. Their principal strengths are reproducibility and experimental tractability, but they incompletely capture intratumoral heterogeneity, stromal co-evolution, and immune surveillance because long-term cultured lines undergo clonal selection and require host immunosuppression. Nonetheless, comparison of subcutaneous and orthotopic implantation has shown that anatomical context substantially affects invasion and dissemination, with cecal implantation yielding more clinically relevant local growth and metastatic behavior than ectopic sites ref [78], ref [79].

Patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models partially address these limitations by directly engrafting fragments of primary or metastatic CRC into severely immunodeficient hosts, thereby preserving histologic architecture, driver alterations, and aspects of interpatient heterogeneity across passages. Large CRC PDX collections have demonstrated substantial concordance with donor tumors in genomic features and therapeutic sensitivity, supporting their use in preclinical stratification studies ref [80], ref [81]. Importantly, treatment responses in CRC PDX cohorts have mirrored clinically observed genotype-response relationships, including resistance patterns linked to RAS pathway activation and sensitivity in molecularly defined subsets ref [81], ref [82].

Despite these advantages, PDX systems remain constrained by replacement of human stroma with murine components, variable engraftment bias toward aggressive tumors, cost, and limited capacity to model adaptive immunity. Their utility is therefore greatest when integrated with orthotopic transplantation, longitudinal molecular profiling, and co-clinical trial designs. Recent work using metastatic CRC PDX and matched organoid-xenograft platforms further suggests that combining patient-derived models can improve prediction of treatment response while retaining in vivo assessment of tumor architecture and drug exposure ref [82], ref [23].

Overall, xenograft and PDX models occupy a central translational niche in CRC research: they are less faithful than endogenous genetically engineered models for tumor initiation, but more directly relevant for evaluating human tumor dependencies, therapeutic vulnerabilities, and, when implanted orthotopically or derived from metastatic lesions, determinants of colonization and progression ref [79], ref [80], ref [23].

subsections.section_title: In Vivo Models of Colorectal Cancer: From Tumor Initiation to Metastatic Dissemination
subsections.content:
Orthotopic colorectal cancer models place tumor cells or tissue fragments into the cecal or rectal wall, thereby preserving local stromal architecture, vascular drainage, and exposure to intestinal immune and microbial cues. Compared with subcutaneous implantation, these models more faithfully reproduce invasive growth, regional spread, and spontaneous dissemination to liver and lung, making them especially useful for interrogating later stages of disease progression. Technical refinements in surgical implantation and endoscopic intramural injection have improved reproducibility while enabling longitudinal assessment of primary tumor growth and metastatic outgrowth ref [1], ref [2].

A major strength of orthotopic systems is their capacity to model organotropic metastasis from an anatomically relevant primary site. Classic work showed that implantation of human colon cancer cells into the cecum of immunodeficient mice yields progressive local invasion and distant metastases not observed after ectopic implantation ref [3]. Subsequent studies using patient-derived orthotopic implantation demonstrated that these models can retain histopathologic and metastatic features of the donor tumor, supporting their utility for translational studies of tumor heterogeneity and therapeutic response ref [4].

Experimental metastasis approaches complement orthotopic models when the goal is to isolate specific steps of dissemination. Intrasplenic or portal-vein injection efficiently assays liver colonization, whereas tail-vein injection preferentially tests lung seeding; however, these routes bypass early events such as local invasion and intravasation. Such reductionist models have nevertheless been instrumental in defining metastatic programs in colorectal cancer, including stromal TGF-beta signaling and endothelial interactions that shape hepatic colonization ref [5], ref [6]. More recently, rectal organoid transplantation into immunocompetent mice has provided a tractable platform linking engineered driver mutations to spontaneous metastasis in vivo ref [7].

subsections.section_title: In Vivo Models of Colorectal Cancer: From Tumor Initiation to Metastatic Dissemination
subsections.content:
Humanized animal models aim to overcome a central limitation of conventional xenografts: the inability to study colorectal cancer (CRC) in the presence of a functional human immune system. Most platforms rely on highly immunodeficient recipients such as NSG mice, which support engraftment of human hematopoietic stem cells or peripheral blood mononuclear cells and can subsequently host CRC cell lines or patient-derived tumors. These systems have been used to examine tumor–immune crosstalk, T-cell dysfunction, myeloid-mediated suppression, and responses to immunotherapy in a setting that is more clinically relevant than standard PDX models, although incomplete immune reconstitution and graft-versus-host disease remain major constraints ref [83], ref [84].

For CRC specifically, humanized PDX approaches are particularly valuable for mismatch repair-deficient or microsatellite instability-high tumors, where adaptive immunity strongly shapes therapeutic response. The importance of this context is underscored by clinical studies showing durable activity of PD-1 blockade in mismatch-repair-deficient CRC ref [85], ref [86]. In preclinical work, co-engraftment of human immune cells with patient tumors has enabled analysis of checkpoint blockade, cytokine networks, and stromal remodeling, while preserving key features of inter-patient heterogeneity ref [80], ref [87].

Despite these advantages, current humanized models still incompletely reproduce the human gut mucosal immune compartment, microbiota-dependent inflammation, and metastatic organ tropism that are central to CRC progression. Next-generation strains expressing human cytokines or HLA molecules, together with orthotopic implantation and autologous tumor–immune pairing, are expected to improve fidelity and make these models increasingly useful for mechanistic studies and biomarker-guided testing of immunotherapies in metastatic CRC ref [83], ref [84], ref [88].

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Elucidating Colorectal Cancer Biology
subsections.content:
Experimental models have been central to defining the canonical molecular sequence of colorectal tumorigenesis. Genetically engineered mice carrying Apc lesions established aberrant WNT/β-catenin signaling as an initiating event that is sufficient to drive intestinal adenoma formation, while human molecular studies linked sequential acquisition of KRAS activation, loss of SMAD/TGF-β restraint, and TP53 disruption to progression from adenoma to carcinoma ref [1], ref [2], ref [3]. Together, these systems transformed CRC from a descriptive histopathologic entity into a pathway-based disease model.

Subsequent organoid and in vivo editing approaches refined this framework by showing that combinations of APC, KRAS, TP53, and SMAD4 alterations can reconstruct key stages of malignant transformation and invasive behavior in human intestinal epithelium ref [4]. These models also clarified that pathway output is highly context dependent: oncogenic signaling is shaped by cell-of-origin, differentiation state, and the surrounding niche, helping explain why identical driver mutations can produce divergent phenotypes.

Beyond the classical sequence, experimental models have highlighted pathway convergence across molecular subtypes. Hyperactive EGFR–MAPK and PI3K signaling cooperate with WNT activity, whereas mismatch-repair deficiency creates a hypermutable state that accelerates evolutionary exploration of oncogenic circuits ref [5], ref [6]. More recently, integrated perturbation studies have shown that lineage-specifying transcriptional programs and stromal cues can stabilize distinct signaling states, linking genotype to the consensus molecular subtype architecture observed in patient tumors ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Elucidating Colorectal Cancer Biology
subsections.subsection_title: Cancer Stem Cells and Cellular Plasticity
subsections.content:
Experimental models have been central to defining cancer stem cell (CSC) hierarchies in colorectal cancer (CRC) and to showing that stemness is a functional state rather than a fixed cellular identity. Early xenotransplantation studies demonstrated that only rare subpopulations marked by CD133 could efficiently initiate tumors, supporting the existence of tumor-propagating cells in human CRC ref [89]. Subsequent lineage-tracing and organoid-based studies refined this view by showing that Lgr5-positive cells are highly tumorigenic and can sustain adenoma and carcinoma growth, mirroring the role of normal intestinal stem cells in tissue maintenance ref [90], ref [91].

At the same time, CRC models have revealed striking cellular plasticity within these hierarchies. Ablation of Lgr5-positive cells in established tumors does not abolish tumor growth permanently, because differentiated progeny can reacquire stem-like features and repopulate the CSC pool ref [92]. This dynamic interconversion is strongly shaped by niche-derived signals: hepatocyte growth factor from stromal cells and osteopontin from the tumor microenvironment potentiate Wnt signaling and reinforce clonogenic, stem-like behavior in colon cancer cells ref [93], ref [94].

These findings have shifted the field from a rigid CSC model to a state-transition framework in which genetic lesions, developmental programs, and microenvironmental cues jointly regulate tumor-propagating capacity. Single-cell analyses further support this interpretation by identifying coexisting proliferative, regenerative, and differentiated malignant states within individual CRCs, with therapeutic implications for resistance and relapse ref [95].

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Elucidating Colorectal Cancer Biology
subsections.content:
Experimental models have been central to defining how colorectal cancer (CRC) progression depends on reciprocal signaling between neoplastic epithelium and the surrounding stroma. Genetically engineered and orthotopic mouse models showed that myofibroblast- and fibroblast-derived signals are not passive by-products of tumor growth but active determinants of stemness, invasion, and therapeutic response. In particular, stromal secretion of hepatocyte growth factor can restore Wnt activity in differentiated CRC cells and re-establish tumor-initiating capacity, illustrating how niche cues reshape epithelial cell state ref [96].

Organoid co-culture systems further clarified the bidirectional nature of this crosstalk. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) provide redundant growth factors, extracellular matrix components, and cytokines that can substitute for canonical epithelial niche requirements and sustain CRC organoid growth under restrictive conditions ref [97], ref [98]. These platforms also revealed marked CAF heterogeneity, with distinct fibroblast states differentially linked to matrix remodeling, TGF-beta signaling, and poor prognosis, findings that were reinforced by single-cell analyses of human CRC specimens ref [99].

Beyond fibroblasts, experimental depletion and imaging studies established a broader multicellular microenvironmental program in which macrophages, endothelial cells, and TGF-beta-responsive stromal compartments cooperate to promote immune exclusion and metastatic competence ref [100], ref [101]. More recent integrated single-cell maps suggest that conserved multicellular 'ecosystems' spanning epithelial, stromal, and immune compartments recur across patients and may be more predictive of outcome than any single cell type alone ref [102]. Together, these models position stromal crosstalk as a causal layer of CRC biology rather than a secondary histologic feature.

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Elucidating Colorectal Cancer Biology
subsections.content:
Experimental models have been central to linking chronic mucosal inflammation with colorectal tumorigenesis. In genetically susceptible mice, epithelial barrier failure and innate immune dysregulation create a cytokine-rich niche that promotes dysplasia, while interleukin-6/STAT3 and NF-κB signaling integrate inflammatory cues with epithelial survival and proliferation. This principle was established in colitis-associated cancer models showing that enterocyte IKKβ and myeloid-cell inflammatory programs cooperatively drive tumor promotion, and that STAT3 activity in intestinal epithelium is a key effector of regeneration-to-neoplasia transitions ref [103], ref [104].

Microbiota-focused models further demonstrated that tumor-promoting inflammation is not simply host intrinsic but ecologically conditioned. Germ-free and gnotobiotic studies showed that microbial communities regulate adenoma burden and shape anti-tumor immunity, while specific pathobionts can act as direct oncogenic cofactors. Enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis induces Th17-polarized inflammation and colon tumor formation in Min mice, and pks+ Escherichia coli strains produce the genotoxin colibactin that leaves a distinctive mutational imprint in human colorectal cancer, connecting bacterial exposure to genome damage ref [105], ref [106], ref [107].

These models support a mucosal-ecology view of colorectal cancer in which epithelial genotype, mucus and barrier integrity, immune tone, and microbial metabolism are interdependent. Preclinical work also indicates that microbiota composition influences therapeutic response; commensal depletion can blunt the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade, whereas defined bacterial consortia restore anti-tumor immunity in vivo ref [108]. Together, experimental systems have reframed inflammation and the microbiota from contextual modifiers to active determinants of colorectal cancer initiation, progression, and treatment sensitivity.

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Elucidating Colorectal Cancer Biology
subsections.content:
Experimental models have been central to defining colorectal cancer (CRC) metastasis as an evolutionary process shaped by both tumor-intrinsic programs and host-organ selection. Genetically engineered and orthotopic transplantation models showed that dissemination can arise from late-emerging subclones with enhanced fitness, while phylogenetic analyses of matched primary and metastatic lesions further supported branched evolution and substantial intermetastatic diversity rather than simple linear spread ref [109], ref [4]. Functional studies in mice also demonstrated that metastatic competence is not solely explained by growth rate, but by traits enabling invasion, survival in circulation, and colonization of permissive niches ref [110].

Organ tropism has been especially well interrogated in liver-directed CRC models, reflecting the dominant clinical pattern of portal venous dissemination. In vivo selection approaches identified niche-adaptive programs that facilitate hepatic seeding, including stromal remodeling, endothelial interactions, and hepatocyte-derived trophic signaling ref [111]. Patient-derived organoids and xenografts have extended these observations by showing that metastatic outgrowth depends on context-specific dependencies not always evident in the primary tumor, thereby offering tractable systems to model liver colonization and therapy response ref [23].

Metastatic models have also clarified how route of dissemination and microenvironmental filtering influence tropism beyond the liver. Studies of circulating tumor cell clusters and collective dissemination indicate that multicellular emboli possess enhanced metastatic efficiency, helping explain rapid seeding of distant organs ref [112]. More broadly, evolutionary analyses of treated metastatic CRC revealed continued diversification under therapeutic pressure, emphasizing that organ colonization and resistance are coupled processes that should be studied longitudinally across sites and model systems ref [113].

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Elucidating Colorectal Cancer Biology
subsections.content:
Experimental models have been central to showing that colorectal cancer (CRC) evolves as a branched, rather than strictly linear, process. Multiregion sequencing of primary tumors and matched metastases demonstrated pervasive spatial heterogeneity, with early truncal driver events such as APC, KRAS, and TP53 overlaid by region-specific private alterations, supporting parallel subclonal diversification during progression ref [114]. In patient-derived organoids, many of these genomic and phenotypic differences are retained ex vivo, enabling controlled testing of how distinct clones differ in growth, lineage state, and drug response ref [16].

Lineage-tracing and genome-editing studies in mouse and organoid systems further indicate that clonal competition is dynamic and shaped by both intrinsic fitness and niche context. In normal intestine, neutral drift among equipotent stem cells provides a baseline evolutionary framework ref [115], whereas introduction of oncogenic mutations biases crypt fixation and enables selective sweeps. Combinatorial CRISPR-based modeling in organoids has been especially useful for reconstructing stepwise tumor evolution and quantifying how specific mutational combinations alter clonal behavior ref [28].

These models also clarify why heterogeneity matters therapeutically. Xenograft and organoid studies show that minor pre-existing subclones can survive targeted or cytotoxic therapy and seed relapse, while single-cell analyses reveal transcriptional plasticity superimposed on genetic diversification ref [2,5]. At the metastatic stage, phylogenetic analyses support both monoclonal and polyclonal seeding patterns, indicating that dissemination itself can preserve or reshape intratumoral diversity ref [1,6]. Together, experimental CRC models provide a tractable platform for linking genotype, cell state, and ecological selection during clonal evolution.

subsections.section_title: Translational and Therapeutic Applications of Colorectal Cancer Models
subsections.subsection_title: Preclinical Drug Screening and Efficacy Testing
subsections.content:
Preclinical drug screening in colorectal cancer (CRC) has progressively shifted from conventional 2D cell lines toward model systems that better preserve tumor architecture, clonal heterogeneity, and clinically relevant drug responses. Large pharmacogenomic studies established the utility of CRC cell-line panels for linking genotype to drug sensitivity, but also highlighted the limited translational fidelity of homogeneous in vitro systems for predicting patient benefit ref [33], ref [118]. This prompted broader adoption of three-dimensional patient-derived organoids and xenografts as intermediate platforms for efficacy testing.

Patient-derived CRC organoids support scalable testing of cytotoxic, targeted, and combination therapies while retaining major histologic and molecular features of the source tumor. In landmark studies, organoid biobanks recapitulated differential responses to EGFR-, MAPK-, and HER-pathway inhibition and showed concordance with genotype-guided therapeutic vulnerabilities, supporting their use for prioritizing regimens before in vivo validation ref [16], ref [13]. Complementarily, patient-derived xenografts preserve stromal context and pharmacologic exposure in vivo, and comparative analyses demonstrated that treatment responses in xenografts can parallel outcomes observed in the clinic, reinforcing their value for go/no-go decisions in translational pipelines ref [119], ref [120].

An effective preclinical screening strategy therefore relies on model complementarity: high-throughput organoid or cell-line screening to identify active compounds, followed by xenograft-based confirmation of antitumor efficacy, dosing schedules, and combination tolerability. Recent co-clinical efforts further indicate that organoid drug testing can mirror patient responses to standard and investigational agents, strengthening the rationale for integrating these models into preclinical efficacy testing frameworks for CRC ref [121].

subsections.section_title: Translational and Therapeutic Applications of Colorectal Cancer Models
subsections.content:
Experimental colorectal cancer models are central to dissecting both primary and acquired resistance to systemic therapy. Patient-derived organoids and xenografts preserve interpatient heterogeneity and frequently recapitulate clinical responses to EGFR blockade, chemotherapy, and targeted agents, enabling longitudinal study of resistant subclones under treatment pressure ref [23], ref [13]. These platforms have been particularly informative for distinguishing intrinsic resistance driven by baseline oncogenic lesions from adaptive resistance that emerges through clonal selection or signaling rewiring.

Work in these models has clarified that resistance to anti-EGFR therapy is commonly mediated by alterations in the MAPK pathway, including KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, and EGFR extracellular-domain mutations, many of which can be detected in circulating tumor DNA during therapy and modeled functionally ex vivo ref [122], ref [123]. Parallel studies using patient-derived systems also showed that rare pre-existing KRAS-mutant subclones can expand during cetuximab exposure, providing a mechanistic basis for transient responses and subsequent relapse ref [124]. More broadly, integrated genomic and pharmacologic profiling of colorectal cancer organoids demonstrated how genotype-context dependencies shape sensitivity and cross-resistance across drug classes ref [16].

Resistance modeling is also valuable for testing rational salvage strategies. In BRAF(V600E)-mutant colorectal cancer, preclinical models anticipated the limited activity of BRAF inhibition alone and supported combined vertical blockade of BRAF, EGFR, and MEK as a means to suppress feedback reactivation of EGFR-MAPK signaling ref [125]. Thus, resistance-focused model systems do not merely explain treatment failure; they provide experimentally tractable platforms for anticipating evolutionary escape routes, validating resistance biomarkers, and prioritizing combination regimens for clinical translation.

subsections.section_title: Translational and Therapeutic Applications of Colorectal Cancer Models
subsections.content:
Biomarker discovery in colorectal cancer (CRC) increasingly relies on model systems that preserve patient-specific molecular heterogeneity while enabling controlled perturbation. Patient-derived organoids are especially valuable because they retain key genomic and phenotypic features of the source tumors, allowing candidate predictive biomarkers to be linked directly to drug response and pathway dependence ref [23], ref [16]. In parallel, large-scale pharmacogenomic studies in CRC cell-line panels have provided orthogonal evidence that recurrent alterations in RAS, BRAF, PIK3CA, mismatch repair, and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling can stratify therapeutic sensitivity and resistance, thereby helping to prioritize biomarkers for downstream clinical validation ref [126].

Validation requires moving beyond correlation to reproducibility across models and concordance with patient outcomes. Xenograft and organoid platforms have been used to test whether putative biomarkers remain informative in more physiological settings, including for anti-EGFR therapy where KRAS mutation status emerged as a robust negative predictor of cetuximab benefit ref [127]. More recently, transcriptomic subtype frameworks such as the consensus molecular subtypes (CMS) have provided a higher-order biomarker layer that can be interrogated in experimental models for associations with stromal interaction, prognosis, and treatment response ref [2]. These approaches are particularly useful for distinguishing prognostic markers from genuinely predictive ones.

Experimental models also support biomarker refinement through longitudinal sampling and functional editing. Genome engineering in organoids enables direct testing of whether candidate alterations are causal determinants of phenotype, while serial derivation from treatment-naive and resistant lesions can reveal dynamic biomarkers such as emergent MAPK-pathway lesions or HER2 amplification ref [16], ref [128]. Clinically, this functional-validation pipeline complements tissue and liquid-biopsy assays and is exemplified by biomarker-guided anti-EGFR rechallenge strategies informed by circulating tumor DNA profiling of resistant clones ref [129].

Together, these platforms position CRC models not merely as descriptive systems, but as intermediaries that connect molecular observations to analytically and clinically validated biomarkers.

subsections.section_title: Translational and Therapeutic Applications of Colorectal Cancer Models
subsections.content:
Immunotherapy evaluation in colorectal cancer (CRC) models must capture the strong dependence of clinical benefit on tumor immunogenicity and microenvironmental context. Clinically, mismatch repair-deficient/microsatellite instability-high (dMMR/MSI-H) CRC shows marked sensitivity to PD-1 blockade, whereas most microsatellite-stable tumors remain refractory, establishing a benchmark for preclinical modeling ref [85], ref [130]. Accordingly, experimental systems are most informative when they preserve neoantigen load, interferon signaling, antigen presentation, and stromal–immune interactions rather than tumor epithelium alone.

Conventional patient-derived organoids are valuable for testing tumor-intrinsic determinants of immune response, but their major translational advance has come from co-culture formats incorporating autologous lymphocytes or peripheral immune cells. Such platforms can support expansion of tumor-reactive T cells and permit mechanistic interrogation of checkpoint blockade, antigen-specific killing, and resistance pathways ref [13], ref [131]. In parallel, organotypic air-liquid interface cultures retain endogenous immune and stromal compartments for limited periods, enabling ex vivo assessment of immune checkpoint sensitivity in a more native tissue architecture ref [132].

Murine syngeneic and genetically engineered models remain essential for evaluating systemic immunotherapy effects, including T-cell priming, myeloid suppression, and combinatorial strategies with radiation, targeted therapy, or TGF-beta pathway blockade. Notably, TGF-beta-driven stromal exclusion has emerged as a tractable mechanism of immune evasion relevant to checkpoint resistance ref [133]. More recently, humanized mouse models and patient-derived explants have extended testing to human immune components, although variability in immune reconstitution and short culture windows still constrain prediction. Together, these models are best viewed as complementary tiers for prioritizing regimens, defining biomarkers, and identifying rational combinations for immunologically cold CRC ref [134].

subsections.section_title: Translational and Therapeutic Applications of Colorectal Cancer Models
subsections.subsection_title: Precision Medicine and Functional Personalized Testing
subsections.content:
Precision medicine in colorectal cancer increasingly relies on functional assays that complement genomic profiling by directly measuring patient-specific drug response. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) and ex vivo tumor cultures preserve many histologic, genetic, and pharmacologic features of the originating lesion, enabling prospective testing of standard cytotoxics and targeted agents on clinically relevant timescales. Early studies showed that colorectal cancer organoids retain the mutational landscape of patient tumors and can be used for high-throughput drug sensitivity profiling, thereby providing a practical platform for individualized therapeutic prioritization ref [16], ref [23].

A major translational advance has been the demonstration that organoid drug responses can correlate with clinical outcomes. In metastatic gastrointestinal cancers, including colorectal cancer, prospective interventional studies have shown that treatment selection informed by PDO testing is feasible and can identify therapies associated with clinical benefit in heavily pretreated patients ref [135]. Similarly, co-clinical frameworks using living biobanks linked organoid pharmacotyping to patient response, supporting the use of PDOs as predictive avatars rather than purely descriptive models ref [23], ref [13].

Nevertheless, functional personalized testing remains constrained by sampling bias, variable establishment success, and incomplete representation of stromal, vascular, and immune determinants of response. These limitations have motivated integration with patient-derived xenografts, air-liquid interface systems, and multi-omic biomarkers, as well as efforts to standardize assay turnaround time and response metrics for routine clinical deployment ref [42], ref [39]. In practice, the greatest value of these platforms may lie in resolving therapeutically actionable vulnerabilities when genomic findings are ambiguous or insufficiently predictive ref [135], ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Translational and Therapeutic Applications of Colorectal Cancer Models
subsections.content:
Toxicology-oriented colorectal cancer (CRC) models are increasingly used to balance antitumor efficacy against injury to normal intestinal and extraintestinal tissues. Patient-derived organoids and genetically defined epithelial cultures can reproduce clinically relevant responses to fluoropyrimidines, irinotecan, and oxaliplatin, while matched normal organoids provide a tractable comparator for therapeutic index estimation. In parallel, organoid biobanks and high-throughput platforms have shown that ex vivo drug sensitivity testing can identify exposure ranges and combinations that retain activity across molecular CRC subtypes, thereby informing regimen selection before animal or clinical escalation ref [16], ref [121].

Treatment optimization also depends on modeling host toxicity mechanisms that are difficult to capture in conventional tumor-only systems. Human intestinal organoids have been used to study gastrointestinal epithelial damage, regeneration, and drug-induced barrier dysfunction, which is especially relevant for irinotecan-associated mucositis and combination chemotherapy scheduling ref [136]. Beyond the gut, organ-on-chip approaches incorporating fluid flow and multicellular microenvironments have emerged as a complementary strategy for predicting off-target toxicities and pharmacodynamic interactions more faithfully than static culture systems ref [137].

These platforms are most valuable when integrated with pharmacokinetic and pharmacogenetic knowledge. For fluoropyrimidines, deficiency of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase is a well-established determinant of severe toxicity and now directly informs dose reduction or alternative treatment strategies ref [138]. Likewise, UGT1A1 variation modifies SN-38 exposure and irinotecan toxicity, supporting genotype-aware optimization of dosing intensity ref [139]. Together, functional CRC models and host-specific molecular predictors can improve regimen selection, de-risk combinations, and support adaptive treatment schedules that maximize benefit while minimizing toxicity.

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Emerging Innovations, and Future Directions in Colorectal Cancer Modeling
subsections.content:
Existing colorectal cancer (CRC) models each capture only a subset of disease biology. Conventional 2D cell lines are inexpensive and experimentally tractable, but prolonged in vitro adaptation reshapes clonal composition, signaling dependencies, and drug response, limiting their fidelity to patient tumors [1]. Even large cell-line collections only partially represent the molecular and phenotypic heterogeneity of CRC, especially rare genotypes, differentiation states, and treatment-induced evolution [2].

Animal models offer tissue context but remain constrained by species-specific differences and simplified genetics. Genetically engineered mouse models such as Apc-driven systems have been indispensable for studying intestinal tumor initiation, yet they often emphasize adenoma formation and incompletely model the invasive, metastatic, and immunologically edited stages characteristic of advanced human CRC [3]. Patient-derived xenografts better preserve histology and genomic architecture, but engraftment selects for aggressive subclones and requires immunodeficient hosts, thereby obscuring stromal and immune interactions that are central to therapeutic response [4].

Organoid platforms have improved patient specificity, but they also have important limitations. Although colorectal cancer organoids can retain key genomic features and enable drug testing, standard epithelial organoid cultures underrepresent vasculature, fibroblasts, enteric nerves, microbiota, and dynamic immune crosstalk [5]. More broadly, current preclinical models remain poor at recapitulating metastatic organotropism, treatment-driven plasticity, and the ecological complexity of the tumor microenvironment, underscoring the need for hybrid systems that integrate patient-derived tissue, multicellular context, and longitudinal measurement [6].

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Emerging Innovations, and Future Directions in Colorectal Cancer Modeling
subsections.content:
A persistent barrier in colorectal cancer (CRC) modeling is the limited standardization of experimental inputs, culture conditions, and reporting practices across laboratories. Variability in extracellular matrix composition, growth-factor cocktails, stromal co-culture design, and passage history can substantially alter organoid morphology, clonal selection, and drug response, complicating cross-study interpretation. The establishment of living biobanks of patient-derived CRC organoids has improved access to shared materials, but these studies also highlighted how standardized derivation, annotation, and quality-control workflows are prerequisites for meaningful inter-model comparison ref [38], ref [16].

Reproducibility is further challenged by genomic drift, intratumoral heterogeneity, and inconsistent authentication of model identity. Comparative analyses of patient-derived organoid collections have shown that even when major driver alterations are retained, differences in sampling, culture adaptation, and readout platforms influence pharmacogenomic associations ref [23], ref [144]. Similar concerns apply to xenografts and cell lines, where contamination, lineage misidentification, and nonuniform endpoint definitions have long impaired reliability; broader community guidance on preclinical rigor has therefore emphasized authentication, protocol transparency, and predefined analytical criteria ref [145].

Improving data comparability will require harmonized metadata standards and benchmark datasets that integrate histopathology, genomics, transcriptomics, and functional phenotyping. Large-scale efforts such as the Human Tumor Atlas Network illustrate the value of common ontologies, coordinated tissue processing, and reproducible computational pipelines for linking data across platforms and centers ref [146]. For CRC specifically, consensus reporting of specimen origin, molecular subtype, medium formulation, and response metrics should become routine to enable robust meta-analysis and model-informed translation ref [147].

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Emerging Innovations, and Future Directions in Colorectal Cancer Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Integration of Multi-Omics and Single-Cell Approaches
subsections.content:
Integrating multi-omics with single-cell profiling is increasingly essential for colorectal cancer (CRC) modeling because bulk measurements obscure the epithelial, stromal, and immune heterogeneity that shapes tumor behavior and treatment response. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses have shown that CRC ecosystems contain conserved malignant programs alongside diverse fibroblast and myeloid states, while metastatic lesions can preserve or reconfigure these niches in clinically relevant ways ref [148], ref [149]. Such findings argue that experimental models should be benchmarked not only by histology or driver genotype, but also by their capacity to recapitulate cell-state composition and intercellular signaling networks.

Multi-omic strategies can further connect genotype, epigenetic regulation, transcriptional plasticity, and protein-level phenotypes across CRC evolution. Joint analyses of chromatin accessibility and gene expression at single-cell resolution have revealed regulatory programs underlying colorectal tumor cell identity and lineage bias ref [150], while paired DNA and RNA measurements in organoids and patient-derived systems help distinguish clonal selection from transient adaptive states ref [151]. Spatially resolved transcriptomic approaches add another layer by retaining tissue architecture, thereby identifying how WNT-active tumor zones, immune exclusion, and stromal organization vary across regions that would be homogenized in dissociated samples ref [152].

The major challenge is no longer data generation alone, but robust cross-platform integration. CRC studies increasingly require harmonized workflows for sample processing, batch correction, cell-type annotation, and linkage of single-cell readouts to functional perturbation data. Frameworks for integrated single-cell analysis provide an important computational foundation ref [6], but future CRC models will benefit most when single-cell, spatial, and proteogenomic data are prospectively embedded into organoid, xenograft, and ex vivo validation pipelines, enabling more faithful reconstruction of tumor ecology and therapeutic vulnerability.

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Emerging Innovations, and Future Directions in Colorectal Cancer Modeling
subsections.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) and computational modeling are increasingly important for bridging the gap between high-dimensional colorectal cancer (CRC) data and experimentally tractable hypotheses. In pathology, deep learning has shown near-expert performance for cancer detection and tissue classification in whole-slide images, creating opportunities to quantify gland architecture, stromal composition, and spatial heterogeneity at scales impractical for manual review ref [153]. More broadly, weakly supervised pipelines can infer clinically relevant molecular features directly from histology, suggesting a route to connect morphology in CRC biopsies or organoids with underlying genotype and phenotype ref [154].

Computational models are also reshaping patient stratification and therapeutic prediction. Machine-learning analyses of large molecular cohorts established consensus molecular subtypes (CMS) of CRC, now widely used to contextualize immune infiltration, stromal signaling, and differential drug response across model systems ref [155]. At the same time, mechanistic and network-based approaches provide a complementary framework for linking driver mutations to pathway dynamics and resistance states, particularly when integrated with perturbational or phosphoproteomic data ref [156]. These strategies are especially valuable for comparing cell lines, organoids, and patient tumors, where nominally similar genotypes may occupy distinct regulatory states.

However, progress remains constrained by dataset bias, limited external validation, and poor interoperability across imaging, omics, and functional assays. Foundational reporting principles for prediction models emphasize transparent development, calibration, and independent validation, requirements that remain unevenly met in cancer AI studies ref [157]. Future CRC modeling will likely depend on multimodal architectures that combine digital pathology, single-cell atlases, and longitudinal treatment data, while using interpretable graph- and foundation-model frameworks to improve biological insight rather than merely predictive performance ref [158].

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Emerging Innovations, and Future Directions in Colorectal Cancer Modeling
subsections.content:
Ethical and practical constraints increasingly shape colorectal cancer (CRC) modeling. Animal studies remain important for interrogating tumor–microenvironment and metastatic interactions, but they are limited by welfare concerns, cost, long timelines, and species-specific biology that can reduce translational relevance. The 3Rs framework has therefore become more than a regulatory principle; it is a design imperative that encourages replacement or reduction of animal use through organoids, ex vivo cultures, and microphysiological systems while reserving in vivo work for questions that cannot be addressed otherwise ref [159], ref [160].

Human-derived CRC models introduce a different set of obligations. Patient organoids and biobanks raise issues of informed consent, governance of secondary use, return of clinically meaningful findings, privacy protection for linked genomic data, and equitable access to samples and resulting therapies. These concerns are amplified when living biobanks are connected to molecular and clinical metadata at scale, making robust custodianship and transparent access policies essential for trustworthy translational research ref [82], ref [121].

Practical implementation also affects ethics: sophisticated organoid and organ-on-chip platforms can reduce animal use yet remain expensive, technically demanding, and unevenly distributed across institutions. Variability in extracellular matrices, media formulations, and quality control can undermine reproducibility and create hidden barriers to broad adoption. Recent advances in patient-derived organoid methodology and microengineered gut models highlight both the promise of more human-relevant platforms and the need for scalable, standardized, and affordable workflows if next-generation CRC models are to be both ethically defensible and practically useful ref [13], ref [48].

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Emerging Innovations, and Future Directions in Colorectal Cancer Modeling
subsections.content:
A central future direction in colorectal cancer (CRC) modeling is the development of hybrid systems that deliberately combine the genetic fidelity of patient-derived cultures with the multicellular, biophysical, and immune complexity of in vivo disease. Organoid technology has already shown that patient tumors can be propagated while preserving key histologic and mutational features ref [16], but epithelial-only systems incompletely model stromal signaling, vascular access, and immune editing. Accordingly, next-generation platforms are moving toward composite designs in which tumor organoids are integrated with autologous lymphocytes, fibroblasts, extracellular matrix surrogates, and microfluidic perfusion to better capture therapeutic response and resistance.

Early studies provide proof of principle for this strategy. Air-liquid interface cultures can preserve endogenous immune and stromal compartments in patient tumor organoids ref [13], while coculture systems have enabled expansion of tumor-reactive T cells against autologous CRC organoids ref [161]. Parallel advances in organ-on-chip engineering show that microphysiological devices can recapitulate human intestinal architecture, flow, and host-microbe interactions ref [162], creating a framework for coupling CRC epithelium to controlled vascular, microbial, or drug-delivery modules. These approaches are especially attractive for modeling metastatic dissemination and treatment-induced ecosystem remodeling, which are poorly represented in conventional monocultures.

The most powerful hybrid models will likely be modular and iterative: patient-derived organoids for genotype-specific biology, chip-based platforms for spatial and pharmacologic control, and orthotopic or humanized mouse settings for systemic validation. Recent work using metastasis-derived organoids to study CRC progression underscores the translational value of pairing ex vivo models with in vivo functional testing ref [163]. More broadly, constructing living biobanks linked to clinical and molecular annotation provides the substrate for such integrated pipelines ref [23]. The major challenge now is not only technical assembly, but standardizing readouts so that hybrid models become comparable, scalable, and genuinely decision-relevant.
